# Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment

Shumao Wu Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center,University of
Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: <smwu@cnic.cn>    Kongcheng Zhang
Affiliation: Zhejiang University Email: <zhangkc@zju.edu.cn>   
Jianqiang Huang Email: <jqhuang@cnic.cn>    Baisheng Lai ^(†)^(†)thanks:
Corresponding author: bslai@cnic.cn Email: <bslai@cnic.cn>
Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of
Sciences

###### Abstract

Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed
attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards
struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or
suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy
trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and
used as process supervision signals. Based on this insight, we propose
Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), which leverages self-derived
process rubrics for dense token-level supervision, thereby augmenting
outcome-centric reinforcement learning. Specifically, the current policy
independently generates multiple rubric bundles at each step according
to the same group of trajectories, extracting candidate process rubrics
from cross-trajectory behavioral differences. A frozen verifier then
evaluates all rubric items against each trajectory in the group, and
selects one candidate bundle based on bundle-level alignment between
rubric satisfaction and task success. ORSD treats the selected rubric
bundle as privileged information during training, then compares the
log-likelihoods of the original tokens with and without the rubric. The
resulting likelihood gap provides token-specific process credit, which
is added to the original trajectory-level GRPO advantage through
additive advantage shaping. ORSD thus bridges trajectory-level outcome
supervision and fine-grained process supervision, enabling token-level
credit assignment using process signals. Extensive experiments on
ALFWorld and WebShop show that ORSD accelerates policy improvement and
boosts final task performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B under the
same environment-interaction budget. Our code is available at
[https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD](https://github.com/AnnaXChun/ORSD).

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in web
interaction ([Zhou et al., 2024a](#bib.bib35)) and software
engineering ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)), with applications
extending to embodied exploration ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)). Yet
reliable decision-making in interactive environments remains
challenging: agents must plan sequences of actions, explore unfamiliar
situations, and reflect on feedback to revise unsuccessful strategies.
Recent progress in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)
offers a promising training approach. DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)) shows that verifiable reward feedback can
substantially improve reasoning performance, with reflection and
self-verification emerging during reinforcement learning. Building on
these advances, agentic RL has also adopted Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) to train agents
through environment interaction, as demonstrated by RAGEN ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)) in multi-turn tasks.

Despite these advances, relying solely on outcome rewards provides
limited guidance about which intermediate decisions deserve credit.
Under trajectory-level GRPO, all policy-generated tokens within a
trajectory share the same advantage, so useful actions, redundant steps,
and recoverable mistakes receive the same learning signal. To assign
credit to individual steps, GiGPO ([Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib2))
groups actions from matching environment states across trajectories and
estimates step-level advantages through within-group comparisons. This
refines credit across decisions, although tokens within each action
still share the same step-level signal. More recently, natural-language
rubrics have emerged as another source of supervision by making
task-specific evaluation criteria explicit. Rubrics as Rewards ([Gunjal
et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) use these criteria to construct reward
signals. RLCF ([Viswanathan et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)) constructs
instruction-specific checklists in advance and aggregates
criterion-level judgments into a response score, while OpenRubrics ([Liu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) derives rubrics from existing preference
pairs and trains a rubric-guided reward model for preference
optimization. Although rubric-based methods introduce richer evaluation
criteria, their feedback usually still remains at the trajectory level,
leaving credit assignment to specially individual tokens unresolved.
Moreover, their rubric construction is separate from the policy’s
ongoing learning process, so the criteria are not continually updated by
the updated policy.

These limitations motivate the use of rubrics as privileged context for
finer-grained credit assignment. Our core insight is that comparing the
log-probabilities assigned to the same sampled tokens with and without
rubrics can turn rubric-based guidance into token-level advantages. Such
signals can refine trajectory-level advantages, allowing tokens within
the same trajectory to receive different credits. Moreover, as the
policy evolves during training, its exploration patterns and failure
modes may also change. Generating rubrics online from on-policy
trajectories allows them to reflect the policy’s current behavior,
capturing task-specific constraints, failure patterns, and successful
action sequences that static rubrics may overlook. This enables the
credit assignment signal to adapt to the evolving policy rather than
relying on fixed, predefined criteria. However, jointly deriving rubrics
from on-policy experience and leveraging them as privileged context for
token-level credit assignment remains underexplored.

In this work, we introduce Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), a
framework that turns on-policy experience into adaptive process
supervision for token-level credit assignment. ORSD reuses these
trajectories to construct process supervision in three steps. First,
conditioned on both task prompt and the group of trajectories, the same
policy independently generates multiple rubric bundles, each containing
multiple criteria for evaluating intermediate states along the
trajectories. Second, ORSD employs a verifier to assess the satisfaction
of each rubric criterion on every trajectory, producing a satisfaction
profile for each rubric bundle. It then measures the alignment between
each satisfaction profile and the outcome rewards, and selects the
rubric bundle with the highest correlation as privileged information.
Third, ORSD augments the prompt with the selected privileged information
and recomputes the token likelihoods of the sampled trajectories. The
gap between the original and augmented token likelihoods is then used to
compute the token-level advantage. As a result, ORSD transforms a group
of on-policy trajectories into token-level credit, requiring neither
additional rollouts nor additional environment interactions.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD), a framework that
  uses online-generated process rubrics to derive token-level credit.
  These rubrics are distilled from the policy’s own rollouts and serve
  as privileged information that augments the replay context, with
  token-level log-probability differences between replay with and
  without the rubrics underpinning this fine-grained credit allocation.
- •
  To address the quality variation among generated rubrics, we propose a
  rubric-reward alignment mechanism that filters out low-value rubrics
  by measuring the alignment between rubric satisfaction and task
  success, thereby enhancing the quality of token-level credit.
- •
  Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B show
  that ORSD improves overall success over GRPO under the same
  environment-interaction budget. Ablations support the contributions of
  online rubric generation and rubric–reward alignment.

## 2 Related Work

#### RLVR for LLM Agents.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses automatically
verified outcomes to train language models. PPO and GRPO are commonly
used for policy optimization, with GRPO estimating relative advantages
within groups of sampled responses ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib14);
[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)). For LLM agents, training involves
multiple rounds of interaction, during which policy’s decisions affect
subsequent observations and the final reward. RAGEN examines learning
dynamics in multi-turn agent RL, and Agent Lightning provides a
framework for training agents from their execution traces ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26); [Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)). The environment
interaction also supports additional learning signals. EnvRL uses state
transitions for representation learning, while T²PO adjusts exploration
through uncertainty estimates and turn-level resampling ([Wang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib25); [Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22)).

#### Credit Assignment in Agentic RL.

Credit assignment assigns different credit to individual steps or tokens
in an agent trajectory. GiGPO groups steps across trajectories by state
similarity and estimates relative advantages within each group ([Feng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). HGPO further groups steps according to their
interaction contexts ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). ArCHer uses rewards
from subsequent interactions to estimate the value of the entire
response generated at the current turn, then uses this estimate to
update the policy that generates the response ([Zhou et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib36)). POAD further considers the role of individual
tokens within an action: it treats action generation as a sequence of
token-level decisions and estimates future rewards for each token,
providing a finer-grained training signal ([Wen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)). SC-GRPO conditions on verified solutions and weights
token gradients according to the resulting distributional
divergence ([Shan et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)).

#### Natural-language Rubrics.

A natural-language rubric is a set of written criteria specifying which
aspects of a response or reasoning process to evaluate. Prior work uses
rubrics to provide feedback at different levels: Rubrics as Rewards
assigns a reward to the entire response based on rubric
satisfaction ([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)); Rubrics to Tokens
estimates the relevance of each criterion to individual response tokens,
providing token-level feedback ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)); and
Step-wise Rubric Rewards checks whether each reasoning step satisfies
the criteria and assigns step-level rewards ([Xie et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)). These methods use rubrics to construct fine-grained
supervision, with criteria generated offline and held fixed. We further
investigate how to generate rubrics online that better match the current
policy and use them for token-level credit assignment.

#### On-policy Distillation with Privileged Context.

Knowledge distillation trains a student model using teacher predictions,
with supervision applied to individual tokens or complete
sequences ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib6); [Kim & Rush,
2016](#bib.bib9)). Training can also use data generated by the learner
itself: DAgger collects supervision at states visited by the learner’s
policy ([Ross et al., 2011](#bib.bib13)), while GKD ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1)) trains on student-generated sequences with supervision
provided by a teacher. OPSD ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)) uses the
same model for self-distillation: the model first generates a response,
then computes its log-probability given additional information to
provide a training signal for the original policy. This additional
information is called privileged context. Prior work also extracts such
information from task execution records: Skill-SD ([Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib23)) summarizes experience from completed trajectories
into natural-language skills, while SDPO ([Hübotter et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)) uses environmental feedback and successful attempts
for self-distillation.

## 3 Method

In this section, we present the proposed Online Rubric Self-Distillation
(ORSD), a framework that turns on-policy rollouts into rubrics and then
into token-level credit signals. As shown in
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
at each training step, the current policy first samples a group of
trajectories for the same task and obtains a reward for each trajectory.
It then generates candidate rubric bundles from the task description and
these trajectories. The rubric-reward alignment mechanism selects the
bundle whose rubric satisfaction scores correlate most strongly with the
rewards across the group. Finally, the token-wise log-likelihood
difference between rollouts with and without the selected bundle enables
per-token advantage shaping of the original trajectory-level advantage.
In this way, ORSD reuses the same on-policy trajectories for rubric
generation and privileged paired replay to derive token-specific credit
without introducing additional environment interactions.

![Refer to caption](2611.06543v1/orsd-pipeline.png)

Figure 1: The overview of ORSD. (a) For each task, the policy first
samples a group of trajectories. It then takes the task description and
these trajectories as inputs to generate multiple rubric bundles. (b)
Each Rubric bundle is evaluated on every trajectory, the rubric bundle
with the largest rubric-reward alignment score is selected. (c) The
selected rubric bundle is used to augment the context and compute the
per-token likelihood gap between augmented and non-augmented contexts,
enabling per-token advantage shaping of the original trajectory-level
advantage.

### 3.1 Preliminaries

Let $`\pi_{\mathrm{old}}`$ denote the policy used to sample trajectories
in the current step. For a task $`x`$, ORSD samples $`N`$ trajectories:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{T}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\qquad\tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot\mid x).
``` |  | (1) |

The reward for trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$ is
$`r_{i}=R_{\mathrm{train}}(\tau_{i})`$, as defined in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5 "Reward Definition ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment").
As in GRPO, ORSD normalizes rewards within each task group to obtain a
trajectory-level advantage, which serves as the base advantage for
subsequent token-level advantage shaping ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{num}}}.
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`\mu_{r}`$ and $`\sigma_{r}`$ are the mean and sample standard
deviation of the group rewards. ORSD will add a token-level correction
to this advantage.

### 3.2 Online Rubric Bundle Generation and Selection

Building on the same-task rollout group mentioned above, ORSD further
exploits the behavioral distinctions across trajectories to construct
process supervision. For example, in WebShop, one trajectory may verify
product attributes before purchasing, whereas another may skip this step
and end up selecting an item that does not satisfy the user’s request.
These behavioral differences can be summarized as natural-language
process rubrics. At each training step, we provide the current policy
with the task description $`x`$, the sampled trajectory group
$`\mathcal{T}`$, and a rubric-generation instruction $`p_{r}`$, and
independently sample $`M`$ candidate rubric bundles:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{B}^{(m)}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot\mid x,\mathcal{T},p_{r}),\qquad m=1,\ldots,M.
``` |  | (3) |

Each bundle contains a set of process criteria, denoted by
$`\mathcal{B}^{(m)}=\{\kappa_{k}^{(m)}\}_{k=1}^{K^{(m)}}`$, where the
superscript $`(m)`$ indexes the candidate bundle, $`k`$ indexes a
criterion within it, and $`K^{(m)}`$ is its number of criteria.

Different from prior works, our method produces candidate rubric bundles
online using the policy instead of human-defined criteria or generation
by stronger models. This mechanism enables the generated rubrics to
capture the dynamics of on-policy trajectories, while the challenge is
that candidate rubric bundles exhibit variable quality. To address this,
we select one rubric bundle among the candidates based on a
rubric–reward alignment score. Specifically, a verifier $`V`$ first
scores each trajectory against each criterion $`\kappa_{k}^{(m)}`$:

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       S_{i,k}^{(m)}=V(x,\tau_{i},\kappa_{k}^{(m)})\in[0,1].
       ```                                                    |     | (4) |

For trajectory $`i`$, we average the criterion-level scores
$`S_{i,k}^{(m)}`$ to obtain the bundle-level satisfaction score
$`s_{i}^{(m)}`$:

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{i}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{K^{(m)}}\sum_{k=1}^{K^{(m)}}S_{i,k}^{(m)}.
       ```                                                              |     | (5) |

We then compute the Spearman correlation between bundle satisfaction and
outcome rewards across all $`N`$ trajectories for the task:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho^{(m)}=\operatorname{Spearman}\!\left(\{s_{i}^{(m)}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\right).
``` |  | (6) |

This correlation measures the agreement between the rankings in
$`\{s_{i}^{(m)}\}_{i=1}^{N}`$ and $`\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}`$. Higher
alignment indicates that the bundle better distinguishes higher- and
lower-reward trajectories. Note that to prevent the generated rubrics
from degenerating into simple rules equivalent to outcome rewards,
Equation [3](#S3.E3 "In 3.2 Online Rubric Bundle Generation and Selection ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
does not take outcome rewards as input when generating rubric bundles.
We finally select the bundle with the highest correlation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
m^{\star}=\arg\max_{m}\rho^{(m)},\qquad\mathcal{B}^{\star}=\mathcal{B}^{(m^{\star})}.
``` |  | (7) |

### 3.3 Rubric-Based Advantage Shaping

The selected rubric bundle serves as privileged context for computing
token-level credit. For each policy-generated token $`y_{i,\ell}`$ at
position $`\ell`$ in trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$, let $`y_{i,<\ell}`$ denote
the preceding interaction history, including earlier policy-generated
tokens and environment observations. We compare the log-likelihoods
assigned by $`\pi_{\mathrm{old}}`$ to the same token with and without
the selected rubric:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{i,\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\log\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,\ell}\mid x,\mathcal{B}^{\star},y_{i,<\ell})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,\ell}\mid x,y_{i,<\ell}).`$ |  | (8) |

Both forward passes evaluate the same pre-sampled trajectories, with no
additional sampling. We compute the gap only for policy-generated tokens
and mask environment observations. A positive $`\Delta_{i,\ell}`$
increases the token’s advantage, while a negative value decreases it.
The resulting token-level advantage is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}}=A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\alpha\Delta_{i,\ell}.
``` |  | (9) |

The coefficient $`\alpha\geq 0`$ controls the correction magnitude. Note
that the per-token advantage $`A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}}`$ is derived
from trajectories generated by the policy itself. For this reason, we
categorize ORSD as a self-distillation mechanism that enables
fine-grained credit assignment.

### 3.4 Policy Optimization

We optimize the policy using the token-level advantage
$`A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}}`$ defined in
Eq. equation [9](#S3.E9 "In 3.3 Rubric-Based Advantage Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment").
For each policy-generated token, we define the importance sampling ratio
as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{i,\ell}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,\ell}\mid x,y_{i,<\ell})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,\ell}\mid x,y_{i,<\ell})}.
``` |  | (10) |

The policy is optimized by minimizing the following clipped objective:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ORSD}}(\theta)={}&-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}\sum_{(i,\ell)\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{valid}}}\min\Big\{r_{i,\ell}(\theta)A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}},\\
&\qquad\operatorname{clip}\!\left(r_{i,\ell}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{c},1+\varepsilon_{c}\right)A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}}\Big\}+\eta\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta).\end{split}
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{valid}}`$ denotes the set of valid
policy-generated tokens in the micro-batch, $`\varepsilon_{c}`$ is the
clipping threshold, and $`\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ denotes the KL
regularization weighted by $`\eta`$.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmarks and Metrics.

We evaluate ORSD on ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib19)) and
WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib32)) two long-horizon interactive
benchmarks using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)). For ALFWorld, we report task-wise and overall
success rates on the unseen split. For WebShop, we report the official
task score and success rate.

#### Prompting Baselines.

We include published results for prompting methods that guide
interaction without RL training. ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib33))
interleaves reasoning and actions. Reflexion ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18)) uses reflections on previous attempts to guide later
attempts, while ReflAct ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) relates the
current state to the task goal when choosing actions. ReAct w/
Self-Guidance (SG) adds self-generated guidance during
interaction ([Wang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib24)).

#### Training Baselines.

We compare ORSD with several baselines. (a) GRPO: its training data,
reward definition, thinking mode, rollout count, and the number of
training steps are strictly consistent with ORSD. (b) GiGPO ([Feng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)): it estimates step-level advantages by
grouping actions from similar states. We run GiGPO on both benchmarks
with both Qwen3 backbones. (c) Self-distillation methods, including
OPSD ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)), GRPO+OPSD, and SDAR ([Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). GRPO+OPSD combines GRPO with an auxiliary
distillation loss. The sources of published results and their evaluation
protocols are specified in the notes to
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment").

#### Training Details.

We fine-tune all parameters of both backbones with
VERL/HybridFlow ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). Each run uses four
A100 80GB GPUs. Every update contains eight tasks with eight rollouts
per task. We train for 300 training steps at a learning rate of
$`10^{-6}`$. WebShop episodes allow for at most 15 assistant actions,
while ALFWorld interactions end according to the environment’s
termination conditions. We generate $`M=4`$ candidate rubric bundles per
task and use $`\alpha=0.01`$, $`\varepsilon_{c}=0.2`$, and
$`\eta=10^{-3}`$ by default.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
provides the remaining implementation details.

#### Reward Definition

For ALFWorld, the training reward is the binary task success indicator:

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{\mathrm{train}}(\tau)=\mathbb{I}[\mathrm{success}],
       ```                                                     |     | (12) |

These rewards also form the outcome vector used for bundle selection.
For WebShop, we use

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{train}}(\tau)`$ | $`\displaystyle=0.5R_{\mathrm{env}}(\tau)+0.5\mathbb{I}[R_{\mathrm{env}}(\tau)=1]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-0.05\frac{N_{\mathrm{invalid}}(\tau)}{\max(T,1)}-0.025\frac{N_{\mathrm{loop}}(\tau)}{\max(T,1)}.`$ |  | (13) |

Here, $`R_{\mathrm{env}}(\tau)\in[0,1]`$ is the official WebShop task
score, and $`T`$ counts all attempted environment actions, including
invalid ones. $`N_{\mathrm{invalid}}`$ and $`N_{\mathrm{loop}}`$ count
invalid actions and repeated actions that make no progress. This
training reward is used to compute GRPO advantages and select rubrics on
WebShop. Baselines run in this study use the same reward transformation.
Evaluation only uses the original official metrics, namely the task
score and success rate.

### 4.2 Main Results

ORSD achieves the best overall results across both benchmarks and model
scales. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
ORSD ranks first in ALFWorld overall success and in both WebShop metrics
with Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B. On ALFWorld, ORSD exceeds the strongest
baseline, GRPO, by 12.12 and 3.36 percentage points in overall success
at the two model scales, respectively. On WebShop, ORSD improves success
over the strongest baseline by 2.80 percentage points with Qwen3-1.7B,
compared with GiGPO, and by 10.90 points with Qwen3-4B, compared with
GRPO. The accompanying gains in WebShop score show that the improvement
extends to satisfying the requested product attributes.

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ORSD across household
interaction and web shopping tasks. Its overall gains extend beyond GRPO
to GiGPO and the reported self-distillation baselines, including SDAR.
ORSD derives task-specific process criteria from rollout differences and
uses the selected rubric to refine token-level learning signals through
paired replay. The improvements over GRPO under the same
environment-interaction budget support this approach to extracting
additional supervision from existing trajectories. The following
ablations examine the contributions of online rubric generation and
rubric-reward alignment.

### 4.3 Ablation Study

In this section, we use ablation experiments to examine the
effectiveness of ORSD’s components: online rubric generation, the number
of candidate bundles and their selection, and the advantage shaping
coefficient $`\alpha`$. All ablations use WebShop. We study rubric
generation and selection with both Qwen3 backbones and vary $`\alpha`$
with Qwen3-1.7B.

#### Effectiveness of Online Rubric Generation.

To evaluate the effectiveness of online rubric generation, we construct
an Offline Rubric variant. Before RL training, the initial policy
generates one task-specific rubric bundle for each task, and these
rubrics remain fixed throughout training. As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Effectiveness of Rubric-Reward Alignment. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
Offline Rubric consistently improves over GRPO on both model scales,
confirming that task-specific rubric supervision is already beneficial
even when generated only once. However, it still falls short of online
ORSD by 4.80 percentage points in success rate for both backbones. This
gap highlights the value of refreshing the rubric from the current
policy’s rollouts, so that the supervision remains aligned with the
policy’s changing behavior and failure modes during training.
Importantly, both variants generate rubrics automatically and require no
manually authored criteria.

#### Effectiveness of Rubric-Reward Alignment.

ORSD selects candidate rubric bundles based on their alignment with
outcome rewards. We examine this design through two ablations. ORSD w/o
Rubric-Reward Alignment generates a single bundle and uses it directly,
omitting verifier scoring and candidate selection. Random Rubric retains
the same candidate count as full ORSD ($`M=4`$) but replaces
alignment-based selection with random selection.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Effectiveness of Rubric-Reward Alignment. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
shows that full ORSD outperforms both variants on both model scales.
Relative to the single-bundle variant, ORSD improves success by 2.15 and
9.45 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, respectively. With
the candidate count held fixed, alignment-based selection improves
success over random selection by 3.40 and 7.15 percentage points, with
corresponding score gains of 5.36 and 4.08 points. These consistent
gains demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric-reward alignment in
selecting process supervision for policy training, with the selected
rubrics serving as privileged context for token-level advantage shaping.

|                                  | Qwen3-1.7B |             | Qwen3-4B |             |
|----------------------------------|------------|-------------|----------|-------------|
| Method                           | Score      | Success (%) | Score    | Success (%) |
| Baseline                         | 72.20      | 55.40       | 82.69    | 66.15       |
| Offline Rubric                   | 74.35      | 58.20       | 85.39    | 72.25       |
| ORSD w/o Rubric–Reward Alignment | 77.53      | 60.85       | 83.86    | 67.60       |
| Random Rubric                    | 73.24      | 59.60       | 84.94    | 69.90       |
| ORSD ($`M=4`$)                   | 78.60      | 63.00       | 89.02    | 77.05       |

variants use $`\alpha=0.01`$.

#### Sensitivity to $`\alpha`$.

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Sensitivity to 𝛼. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
compares the default ORSD coefficient $`\alpha=0.01`$ with
$`\alpha=0.001`$ and $`\alpha=0.1`$ on WebShop using Qwen3-1.7B. We
report the success rate and use the same GRPO result as the baseline at
each setting; GRPO corresponds to removing the correction in
Eq. ([9](#S3.E9 "In 3.3 Rubric-Based Advantage Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")).
All three coefficients outperform GRPO, with the default $`\alpha=0.01`$
achieving the highest success rate of 63.00%. These results indicate
that $`\alpha=0.01`$ provides the most effective correction strength
among the tested values, supporting its use as the default setting.

### 4.4 Further Analysis

#### Training Dynamics

Figure 3: Training reward curves comparing ORSD with GRPO on WebShop and
ALFWorld using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B. Both methods use the same
environment-interaction budget.

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Training Dynamics ‣ 4.4 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
compares the training rewards of ORSD and GRPO on both benchmarks and
model scales. On WebShop, ORSD improves earlier with Qwen3-1.7B and
maintains higher rewards through most of training with Qwen3-4B. On
ALFWorld, the advantage is more pronounced at 1.7B and emerges later at
4B. Across all four settings, ORSD achieves higher mean rewards over the
final 300 optimization steps under the same environment-interaction
budget. Together with the gains in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
these results support more effective use of sampled trajectories: ORSD
reuses rollout experience to derive fine-grained supervision through
self-distillation, improving learning without additional environment
rollouts.

#### Analysis of Generated Rubric Bundles

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Analysis of Generated Rubric Bundles ‣ 4.4 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")

selected bundle specifies product attributes and a concrete price
constraint, providing more informative task-specific privileged context
than the rejected candidate’s general criteria. This comparison
illustrates how rubric-reward alignment selects more informative
privileged context to guide token-level advantage shaping.

## 5 Discussion and Limitations

#### Rubric Knowledge is not explicitly accumulated across updates.

ORSD generates task-specific rubrics from the current rollout group at
each update, but does not maintain a persistent repository of previously
discovered criteria. How to retain, refine, and reuse useful rubrics
across training stages and related tasks remains an open question.
Extending ORSD with a rubric memory could support cumulative process
knowledge while preserving adaptation to the evolving policy.

#### Outcome alignment does not fully resolve credit assignment.

ORSD selects rubric bundles by their correlation with trajectory-level
rewards. This objective favors rubrics that distinguish stronger
trajectories, but does not directly optimize their usefulness for
assigning credit within a trajectory. Future work could develop
selection objectives that account for how rubric guidance affects
individual decisions and subsequent policy improvement.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced Online Rubric Self-Distillation (ORSD) to improve credit
assignment in LLM agent reinforcement learning. ORSD generates
task-specific process rubrics online from differences among on-policy
trajectories, without manually authored or fixed offline criteria.
Rubric-reward alignment selects the bundle whose satisfaction scores
best correlate with outcomes. Through privileged paired replay, the
selected rubric converts token-level likelihood gaps into token-level
advantage corrections, providing fine-grained supervision without
additional environment interactions. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop
with Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B show the best overall performance among the
compared methods, while ablations validate online rubric generation and
candidate selection. These results highlight the value of deriving
adaptive process supervision from the policy’s own experience for credit
assignment in long-horizon agent tasks.

## Appendix A Algorithm

1.  1.
    Let $`\pi_{\mathrm{old}}`$ denote the policy used for trajectory
    sampling and paired replay in the current update.
2.  2.
    For every task $`x`$, sample a group of $`N=8`$ trajectories
    $`\mathcal{T}`$ and compute $`A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$.
3.  3.
    Aggregate the task and all trajectories in the group into one
    rubric-generation prompt, then independently sample four complete
    rubric bundles with 5-8 criteria each using the current policy.
4.  4.
    Use the frozen verifier to score every criterion in each complete
    bundle. Average all criterion scores within each trajectory, then
    compute bundle-level Spearman correlation with group outcomes and
    select the complete bundle with the highest score.
5.  5.
    Replay each stored action turn with and without
    $`\mathcal{B}^{\star}`$. Check response masks and token alignment,
    compute the raw $`\Delta_{i,\ell}`$, and add the valid-token
    correction in
    Eq. ([9](#S3.E9 "In 3.3 Rubric-Based Advantage Shaping ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")).
6.  6.
    Accumulate the policy loss and reference-policy KL regularizer in
    Eq. ([11](#S3.E11 "In 3.4 Policy Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment"));
    update the shared policy once.

## Appendix B Prompt Templates

One aggregated prompt supplies the current policy with the task and all
action-observation transcripts in the rollout group. With the group-hint
instruction, the prompt requests a complete process rubric containing
5-8 observable criteria. The policy samples four independent complete
proposals from the same prompt, and each proposal remains intact
throughout selection.

For verification, the frozen verifier receives the task, the rollout
transcripts, and one candidate bundle. Each criterion is scored
independently from visible evidence and receives a satisfaction score in
$`[0,1]`$. All criterion scores in the bundle are averaged within each
trajectory, then correlated with group outcomes across trajectories
using Spearman correlation.

The following templates specify rubric generation and policy interaction
in the two environments. Blue placeholders denote fields populated for
each task. For rubric generation, $`k=8`$ and the previous-attempts
field contains the same-task rollout group.

#### Evaluation and learning curves.

We evaluate every 50 optimizer steps on fixed held-out tasks. Comparison
runs in this study use the same evaluation checkpoints and training
seeds.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Training Dynamics ‣ 4.4 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")
plots training rewards against training steps. Each update collects 64
environment trajectories, so step 300 corresponds to 19,200 training
trajectories. Verifier calls, replay computation, and wall-clock time
are recorded separately.

### C.1 Policy Loss Reduction

The main text uses $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mb}}`$ to denote the masked
micro-batch reduction. Let $`D`$ be the number of data-parallel workers,
$`G`$ the number of gradient accumulation steps per worker, and
$`\mathcal{C}_{d,g}`$ the trajectories in the corresponding micro-batch,
indexed across tasks for this reduction. For any token-level quantity
$`f`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mb}}[f]=\frac{1}{DG}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{d,g}}\sum_{\ell}b_{i,\ell}f_{i,\ell}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{d,g}}\sum_{\ell}b_{i,\ell}}.
``` |  | (14) |

Here, $`b_{i,\ell}`$ is a binary mask for valid response tokens,
excluding prompts, environment observations, and padding. This reduction
first averages over tokens within each micro-batch, then over
micro-batches and workers; it does not separately average over tasks or
turns. The term $`\varepsilon_{\mathrm{num}}`$ ensures numerical
stability when computing GRPO advantages.

### C.2 Paired Replay Data

Paired replay uses records saved at each generation turn. A record
contains the turn index, context messages and token IDs, complete
response token IDs, action-only response history, subsequent
observation, response mask, and rollout log probabilities. Plain replay
packs $`c_{t}+y_{t}`$ independently for each turn. Rubric-conditioned
replay inserts the selected complete bundle into $`c_{t}`$ and reuses
the same target response. The response mask selects the log
probabilities used by the correction. The implementation mask
$`e_{i,\ell}`$ equals one when the tokenization round-trip succeeds,
response tokens align, and both log-likelihoods are finite. A token with
$`e_{i,\ell}=0`$ retains its GRPO advantage. The main-text equations
omit this implementation mask. The policy ratio continues to use the
original context and saved rollout log probabilities.

### C.3 Training entry points and run records

Two launchers under examples/agent_rubric2 define the WebShop group-hint
and ALFWorld first-version group-hint configurations. Both aggregate all
trajectories in a same-task rollout group, sample four complete bundles
with the current policy, select one complete proposal, and apply the raw
additive token correction. GRPO uses the same four-GPU, eight-task,
eight-rollout, 300-step protocol with rubric generation and token
correction disabled.

Rubric generation uses temperature $`0.3`$, top-$`p=0.9`$, and a
4,096-token cap. Verification calls qwen3.5-plus with concurrency 8, at
most four retries, and a 1,536-token output cap. Each run record
contains the API identifier and date, resolved configuration, task IDs,
seeds, saved trajectories, bundle scores, and checkpoint evaluations.
Runs are grouped under verl_rubric_3.

Both replay branches preserve the per-turn context and response IDs,
masks, chat templates, temperature settings, and rubric insertion rules.
Before applying the advantage correction, token scores are written back
to their original response positions. The micro-batch loss reduction and
reference-policy KL settings match GRPO.

## Appendix D Mathematical Form of the Token Correction

#### Effect on trajectory credit.

For $`n_{i}=\sum_{\ell}b_{i,\ell}>0`$, the actual mean advantage is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1}{n_{i}}\sum_{\ell}b_{i,\ell}A^{\mathrm{token}}_{i,\ell}=A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\frac{\alpha}{n_{i}}\sum_{\ell}b_{i,\ell}e_{i,\ell}\Delta_{i,\ell}.
``` |  |

The raw correction can therefore change both the trajectory mean and
individual token signs. Its scale is controlled by $`\alpha`$ and the
replay-alignment mask; no additional normalization or redistribution is
applied.

#### Self-distillation through advantage shaping.

Both terms in $`\Delta_{i,\ell}`$ are computed by the same
$`\pi_{\mathrm{old}}`$. ORSD applies stop-gradient, denoted by
$`\operatorname{sg}`$ below, to the likelihood gap and includes it only
in $`A_{i,\ell}^{\mathrm{token}}`$. At the start of an update, the
additional contribution to the policy-loss gradient is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
-\alpha\,\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mb}}\!\left[e_{i,\ell}\,\operatorname{sg}[\Delta_{i,\ell}]\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,\ell}\mid x,y_{i,<\ell})\right]_{\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}.
``` |  | (15) |

Here, $`\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mb}}`$ denotes the masked micro-batch
reduction in
Eq. ([14](#A3.E14 "In C.1 Policy Loss Reduction ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment")),
applied to the enclosed token-level quantity. Privileged context changes
the weight assigned to each sampled token in the RL update. ORSD
implements privileged self-distillation through advantage shaping;
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}`$ contains no auxiliary KL or
cross-entropy matching objective. The likelihood gap measures the
policy’s response to the selected process context and does not establish
token correctness.
````
